definition: A moral code is a set of standards about right and wrong that is treated as having objective authority. In this historical source, it is contrasted with a code of honour, which is tied more to social position and convention where the two differ.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Honour; pinned source text

reasons: The packet does not explicitly define a “moral code” as “a set of standards about right and wrong” or as “treated as having objective authority.” It only discusses the distinction between a “code of honour” and “the moral code,” and generally notes that people believed in an objective standard of right and wrong, without giving a direct definition of “moral code.”

While the contrast is supported in part (the packet describes “honour” as tied to social stations and rules, and contrasts honour with “ethical right,” noting a mediaeval/modern distinction between “the code of honour and the moral code”), the definition’s phrasing about “objective authority” for the moral code is not substantiated by the packet.
